SUBJECT:  REVIEW AND ADVISORY RECOMMENDATION – ADMINISTRATIVE
  REGULATION NO. 204 (PURCHASING POLICY).

SUMMARY
Administrative Regulation (AR) 204 establishes the City’s requirements for purchasing,
competitive procurement, contracts, public projects, and federally funded expenditures. Finance
has completed a comprehensive update to modernize the policy, reflect implementation of the
City’s new ERP system, and update State and Federal procurement requirements. The
revisions also clarify purchase order and blanket P.O. procedures, contract administration,
cooperative and sole-source purchasing, and replace the automatic five-year contract rebid
requirement with a documented contract review process. Staff recommends that the Finance
Commission review the proposed amendments and recommend approval of the updated AR
204 to the City Council.

RECOMMENDATION
That the Finance Commission review the proposed revisions to Administrative Regulation No.
204 (Purchasing Policy) and provide an advisory recommendation to the City Council for
approval.

DISCUSSION
AR 204 has been updated to reflect the City’s current electronic purchasing and payment
processes. Purchase requisitions, P. O.s, invoices, and financial approvals are now processed
electronically through the ERP, eliminating outdated paper P.O. distribution, claim forms, and
manual approval procedures. The proposed P.O. threshold is increased from $5,000 to $7,500,
while the existing purchasing approval authority remains unchanged.

The blanket P.O. process has also been revised. Blanket P. O.s will be established based on
the total anticipated annual expenditure with a vendor, rather than the amount of an individual
transaction. This ensures the appropriate approval and procurement requirements are applied
to the City’s total anticipated commitment and prevents purchases from being divided to avoid
established thresholds. Contracts are not managed within the ERP. Departments will remain
responsible for contract administration and monitoring, while contracts creating a financial
obligation must be provided to Finance for financial and purchasing review. Fully executed
contracts, amendments, extensions, and renewals must be provided to both Finance and the
City Clerk. Agreements that do not use the City Attorney’s established form, or that materially
modify the City’s standard terms, require City Attorney review and approval as to the form
before execution.
The existing requirement to competitively rebid contracts after five years is proposed to be

  Page 5 of 41

replaced with a Five-Year Contract Review. At five years, the City would either competitively re-
procure the service or document why continuation with the existing provider remains in the
City’s best interest. The review would consider vendor performance, market pricing, available
alternatives, transition and implementation costs, continuity requirements, and other relevant
factors. This maintains periodic oversight while avoiding unnecessary procurement and
transition costs when rebidding is unlikely to provide additional value. A bid which was
completed due to these required practices of bidding once the contract hits 5-years resulted in a
40% increase for a sports park landscape maintenance agreement which had previously had
only CPI as the increaser. The policy also provides clearer guidance for competitive and best-
value procurement, cooperative purchasing, sole-source and single-source purchases, and
standardization. These provisions are intended to provide departments with additional flexibility
while requiring appropriate documentation and preserving competition when reasonably
available.
Finally, the public project and Federal procurement sections have been updated to reference
then-current statutory and Federal thresholds. Current amounts will be included in Exhibit A for
ease of reference, with language recognizing that those thresholds may change. The policy also
clarifies that Federal procurement thresholds determine the required procurement method but
do not change the City’s established expenditure approval authority.
Overall, the proposed amendments modernize AR 204, strengthen internal controls, and
provide clearer and more practical purchasing guidance while maintaining appropriate
competition, transparency, and accountability.

III. DEFINITIONS
For purposes of this Administrative Regulation, the following definitions apply:
Best Value: The overall value to the City determined by considering price and
other relevant factors, which may include quality, qualifications, technical
capability, lifecycle cost, delivery, warranty, service, experience, performance,
risk, implementation requirements, transition costs, and other factors identified in
the procurement.
Blanket Purchase Order: A purchase order established for recurring purchases of
the same general category of goods or services from a vendor during an
approved period, generally a fiscal year. A blanket purchase order shall include
an annual not-to-exceed amount. The total anticipated annual amount, rather
than the value of an individual transaction, determines the applicable approval
and procurement requirements.
Change Order: A written modification to an existing contract, agreement,
purchase order, or public project that changes the price, quantity, schedule,
scope, or other material terms of the original obligation.
Competitive Consideration: A procurement method used for purchases below the
applicable informal procurement threshold in which City staff consider price
reasonableness, available vendors, prior pricing, market conditions, operational
needs, or other relevant information without requiring a formal solicitation.

Contract/Agreement: Any written instrument that creates, modifies, or establishes
legally enforceable rights or obligations between the City and another party.
Contracts and agreements may include professional service agreements, vendor
agreements, leases, licenses, software or subscription agreements, memoranda
of understanding, amendments, extensions, and other contractual documents.
Cooperative Purchase / Piggyback Purchase: A purchase made through a
competitively awarded contract established by another public agency or
recognized cooperative purchasing organization when the originating
procurement permits cooperative use and the City determines the contract is
appropriate for the City's needs.
Direct Payment: A payment processed without issuance of a purchase order
when permitted by this policy or Finance procedures. Direct payments are
processed through the City's ERP system and remain subject to applicable
budget, approval, documentation, aggregation, competitive procurement, and
grant requirements.
Emergency Procurement: A procurement made in response to an unexpected
circumstance requiring immediate action to protect life, health, safety, property,
essential City operations, or another substantial public interest when the delay
associated with normal procurement procedures would be contrary to the City's
interests.
Federal Award: Federal financial assistance received directly from a Federal
awarding agency or indirectly through a pass-through entity, including grants and
cooperative agreements, that is subject to applicable Federal award
requirements, including 2 CFR Part 200.
Formal Procurement: A competitive procurement process generally used when
the anticipated value exceeds the applicable formal procurement threshold.
Formal procurement may include sealed bids, invitations for bids, requests for
proposals, or other methods authorized by applicable law and this policy.
Informal Procurement: A competitive procurement process that does not require
the full procedures of a formal solicitation. Informal procurement generally
includes obtaining quotations or proposals from an adequate number of qualified
sources and documenting the basis for selection.
Lifecycle Cost / Total Cost of Ownership: The total reasonably anticipated cost to
the City over the useful life or term of a purchase or contract, including
acquisition, implementation, installation, licensing, maintenance, operation,
training, consumables, replacement parts, transition, disposal, and other
reasonably foreseeable costs.
Micro-Purchase Threshold (MPT): The then-current Federal micro-purchase
threshold established under applicable Federal law and incorporated into 2 CFR
Part 200. Finance shall maintain the current threshold amount for administrative
reference.

when an exception authorized by applicable law, 2 CFR Part 200, this policy, or
another controlling requirement applies and is properly documented and
approved.

  a. In determining the lowest “responsive” bid, the following

  1. A responsive bid is one which is in substantial conformance
  with the requirements of the invitation to bid, including
  specifications and the City’s contractual terms and
  conditions. Bidders who substitute terms and conditions or
  who qualify their bids in such a manner as to nullify or limit
  their liability shall be considered non-responsive bidders.

  2. Conformance with the requirements of the invitation to bid

  3. The successful bidder must demonstrate the ability to
  successfully fulfill a contract, including rendering of
  subsequent and continuing service. Staff may request proof
  of a prospective bidder’s reliability. Prospective bidders may
  be requested to furnish proof of financial resources, a list of
  current or previous customers, and other pertinent data.
  Such action may also be taken after receipt of bids.
  4. A bidder may be determined to be non-responsive if they fail
  to furnish proof of qualifications when required in a
  reasonable amount of time.
  b. In determining the lowest “qualified” bidder, the following
  elements shall be considered in addition to price:
  1. That the materials, supplies or services offered provide
  the quality, fitness, and capacity for the required usage.
  2. That the bidder has the ability, capacity and skill to
  perform the contract satisfactorily and within the time
  required.
  3. That the bidder’s experience(s) regarding past purchases
  by the City or other public agencies demonstrates the
  reliability of the bidder to perform the contract.
  4. Expected uses of City resources such as staff time to
  assist the selected bidder in fulfilling the contract should

cooperative purchasing arrangements with various governmental agencies, as
well as needing services from vendors and/or professional service firms which
are not routinely available in competitive markets. Accordingly, certain forms of
procurement and/or vendors will use procurement procedures outlined below:
  1.  Governmental/Cooperative Contracts: The City may use a

  and when Finance determines the originating procurement was

  standardization, compatibility, continuity, warranty, unique expertise,

  and required approval. Preference, convenience, incumbent status,

  specific justification needs to be provided for retention and review.

  approval by the City Manager or Finance Director/Finance Division
  Manager or their designees regardless of dollar amount.
  7.  Standardization/Brand Continuity: Standardization may include
  equipment, technology, software, parts, systems, or services when

  integration, warranty, data migration, continuity, or lifecycle-cost
  considerations make standardization advantageous. Standardization
  does not automatically establish a sole source; competition among
  authorized providers should be obtained when practicable. In many
  instances, particularly vehicles maintained by the City, maintenance
  costs have a significant effect on overall cost beyond the purchase
  price. To minimize maintenance costs, the City will often maintain
  parts inventories and tools for a single brand such as Ford. Procuring
  parts and tools for an alternative brand may increase maintenance
  costs significantly which would preclude the lowest price brand
  alternative from being the lowest cost alternative. In instances where
  consistently purchasing a specific brand, will lower maintenance

  Government Code 4525-4529.5, shall follow procedures assuring that

  a. Professional Service Contracts Less Than or Equal to $75,000

  often are entered into based on known expertise and for a
  specific purpose. Going through a competitive bidding process
  for smaller contracts is time consuming and utilizes significantly
  more City resources through staff time than formal competitive
  bidding procedures generate in savings. Contracts $75,000 and
  less in total are considered smaller contracts for this
  consideration and may be procured through competitive
  consideration, informal RFP/RFQ, documented market
  research, or another method appropriate to the nature of the
  services.. Such contracts are not subject to formal bidding
  procedures and will be solicited through an RFQ process

  Professional service contracts that are not for a set amount and
  are so closely tied to the individual contracted that the same
  result would not be expected should the contract be
  competitively bid (services dependent on the individual
  contracted), do not have to be competitively bid. Prime
  examples of this include the City Attorney, City Engineer and
  certain consulting contracts that actually substitute for

  performance; current pricing and market benchmarks; availability

  continuation remains fair, reasonable, and in the City's best
  interest.
  c. Finance may require informal market testing, cooperative pricing
  comparisons, peer-agency contract comparisons, industry
  indices, budgetary quotes, or other evidence of price
  reasonableness.

  a.e.  Federally funded contracts remain subject to 2 CFR Part 200

SUMMARY
Administrative Regulation (AR) 204 establishes the City’s requirements for purchasing,
competitive procurement, contracts, public projects, and federally funded expenditures. Finance
has completed a comprehensive update to modernize the policy, reflect implementation of the
City’s new ERP system, and update State and Federal procurement requirements. The
revisions also clarify purchase order and blanket P.O. procedures, contract administration,
cooperative and sole-source purchasing, and replace the automatic five-year contract rebid
requirement with a documented contract review process. Staff recommends that the Finance
Commission review the proposed amendments and recommend approval of the updated AR
204 to the City Council.

RECOMMENDATION
That the Finance Commission review the proposed revisions to Administrative Regulation No.
204 (Purchasing Policy) and provide an advisory recommendation to the City Council for
approval.

DISCUSSION
AR 204 has been updated to reflect the City’s current electronic purchasing and payment
processes. Purchase requisitions, P. O.s, invoices, and financial approvals are now processed
electronically through the ERP, eliminating outdated paper P.O. distribution, claim forms, and
manual approval procedures. The proposed P.O. threshold is increased from $5,000 to $7,500,
while the existing purchasing approval authority remains unchanged.

The blanket P.O. process has also been revised. Blanket P. O.s will be established based on
the total anticipated annual expenditure with a vendor, rather than the amount of an individual
transaction. This ensures the appropriate approval and procurement requirements are applied
to the City’s total anticipated commitment and prevents purchases from being divided to avoid
established thresholds. Contracts are not managed within the ERP. Departments will remain
responsible for contract administration and monitoring, while contracts creating a financial
obligation must be provided to Finance for financial and purchasing review. Fully executed
contracts, amendments, extensions, and renewals must be provided to both Finance and the
City Clerk. Agreements that do not use the City Attorney’s established form, or that materially
modify the City’s standard terms, require City Attorney review and approval as to the form
before execution.
The existing requirement to competitively rebid contracts after five years is proposed to be

do not change the City’s established expenditure approval authority.

provide clearer and more practical purchasing guidance while maintaining appropriate
competition, transparency, and accountability.

  lifecycle cost, or other substantial City interest. The procurement file
  shall document market research, justification, price reasonableness,
  and required approval. Preference, convenience, incumbent status,
  or lack of planning alone is insufficient.
